title: Alcohol Poisoning Signs: When to Call 911 vs. a Bad Hangover
excerpt: The signs of alcohol poisoning, how to tell it apart from a hangover, what to do while you wait for help, the recovery position, and the myths that put people at risk.
metaDescription: Alcohol poisoning signs to know: confusion, can't wake up, slow breathing, vomiting, seizures. How it differs from a hangover and exactly when to call 911.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol poisoning is a medical emergency, not a bad night. It happens when someone drinks so much, so fast, that the parts of the brain that run breathing, heart rate, body temperature, and the gag reflex start to shut down. The signs to know are **confusion or stupor, being hard or impossible to wake, vomiting while passed out or barely conscious, seizures, slow or irregular breathing, and cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin.** A person does not need to show every sign. If someone has even one of the serious ones, call 911.

**The quick rules:** Never leave a very drunk person alone to "sleep it off." If they're passed out, roll them onto their side so they can't choke if they vomit. Don't give them coffee, a cold shower, or food, and don't make them walk it off. If you aren't sure whether it's alcohol poisoning, treat it as if it is and call for help. The cost of calling when you didn't need to is small. The cost of not calling when you did can be a life.

> **This is not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for emergency care.** **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if** someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, is breathing fewer than about 8 times a minute or has pauses of 10 seconds or more between breaths, has a seizure, is vomiting while unconscious or barely conscious, has blue, gray, or very pale skin or lips, or feels cold and clammy to the touch. If you're unsure and the person is conscious, you can call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) for advice, but if any of the signs above are present, call 911 first.

## What Is Alcohol Poisoning?

Alcohol poisoning (doctors often call it acute alcohol intoxication or alcohol overdose) is what happens when the amount of alcohol in the blood gets high enough to suppress the body's basic life-support systems. Alcohol is a depressant. At low levels it loosens you up. At higher levels it slows reaction time and speech. At very high levels it slows down the brainstem, the part of the brain that keeps you breathing and keeps your heart beating without you thinking about it.

The danger isn't only the alcohol itself. As those automatic systems slow down, a few specific things can go wrong:

- **Breathing slows or stops.** This is the main way alcohol poisoning kills.
- **The gag reflex weakens.** Alcohol irritates the stomach and often causes vomiting. If the person is too far gone to cough or turn their head, they can inhale vomit into their lungs and choke or develop a serious lung infection.
- **Body temperature drops.** Alcohol widens blood vessels near the skin, so you lose heat even though you may feel warm.
- **Blood sugar can fall.** Alcohol interferes with the liver's ability to release sugar into the blood. Very low blood sugar can cause seizures.
- **Heart rhythm can become irregular**, and severe dehydration from vomiting can make things worse.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported that alcohol poisoning kills an average of about six people a day in the United States, and most of those deaths are adults, not teenagers or college students. It's not a problem only for "other people." It can happen to anyone who drinks a lot in a short time, especially on a night with shots, drinking games, or a celebration that gets out of hand.

## The Signs of Alcohol Poisoning

The US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) lists these as the critical signs. Learn them now, while you're sober, so you can recognize them when it counts.

1. **Mental confusion or stupor.** The person is far more out of it than "drunk." They may not know where they are, may not respond to their name, or may be awake but not really responsive.
2. **Difficulty staying conscious, or being unable to wake up.** If you shake them, shout their name, or pinch their shoulder and they don't wake up properly, that's an emergency.
3. **Vomiting,** especially while passed out or half-conscious.
4. **Seizures.**
5. **Slow breathing,** meaning fewer than about 8 breaths a minute.
6. **Irregular breathing,** meaning gaps of 10 seconds or more between breaths.
7. **Slow heart rate.**
8. **Clammy skin.**
9. **Dulled responses,** such as no gag reflex (they don't choke or cough when they should).
10. **Very low body temperature, bluish skin, or paleness,** often most visible on the lips and fingertips.

### How to check someone who's passed out

You don't need medical training to do a quick check. Try this:

- **Try to wake them.** Say their name loudly. Shake their shoulder firmly. If they don't respond, or they mumble and immediately drift off again, they need help.
- **Count their breaths.** Watch their chest or put your hand on it and count for a full minute. Fewer than about 8 breaths, or long pauses between breaths, is a 911 call.
- **Look at their skin and lips.** Blue, gray, or very pale lips or fingertips are a sign that they're not getting enough oxygen.
- **Feel their skin.** Cold, damp, clammy skin is a warning sign.
- **Listen.** Gurgling, choking sounds, or snoring that sounds unusual and labored can mean their airway is partly blocked.

If any of these checks worries you, call 911. Don't wait for every sign to show up.

## Hangover or Alcohol Poisoning? How to Tell the Difference

A lot of people search this after a rough night, either for themselves or for a friend. The key difference is **timing and consciousness**.

Alcohol poisoning happens *during* or shortly *after* drinking, while there's still a lot of alcohol in the blood. A hangover happens *the next day*, after blood alcohol has fallen back toward zero. A hangover feels terrible. Alcohol poisoning is dangerous.

| | Hangover | Alcohol poisoning |
|---|---|---|
| **When it happens** | The next morning or day, as alcohol leaves your system | While drinking or within hours afterward, while blood alcohol is high |
| **Consciousness** | Awake, groggy, tired, but you can talk and think | Confused, unresponsive, or can't be woken up |
| **Breathing** | Normal | Slow, shallow, or with long pauses |
| **Vomiting** | Nausea and possibly vomiting, but you're awake and can protect your airway | Vomiting while passed out or barely conscious |
| **Skin** | May look washed out or sweaty | Cold, clammy, pale, or bluish |
| **Seizures** | No | Possible |
| **What to do** | Rest, fluids, food, time | Call 911 |

### When a "hangover" isn't just a hangover

Most hangovers are miserable but not dangerous, and they fade within a day (see [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) for the usual timeline). But some next-day symptoms deserve medical attention. See a doctor or go to urgent care or the ER if, the morning after drinking:

- You can't keep any fluids down for many hours and you're getting dizzy, very thirsty, or barely urinating.
- You're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, or you have black, tarry stools.
- You have severe belly pain, especially pain that spreads to your back.
- You're confused, you can't stay awake, or someone around you says you're "not making sense."
- You have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle (see [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking)), or trouble breathing.
- You have a seizure.

And if you usually drink heavily most days and you get shaky, sweaty, very anxious, or start seeing or hearing things a day or two after you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so get medical care rather than waiting it out. Our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains the difference between ordinary morning-after tremor and the kind that needs a doctor.

## What to Do if You Think Someone Has Alcohol Poisoning

If you think someone has alcohol poisoning, here's what to do, in order.

### 1. Call 911

Do this first if they can't be woken, are breathing slowly or irregularly, are having a seizure, or have blue or very pale skin. Tell the dispatcher how much you think they drank, over how long, and whether they may have taken anything else (pills, cannabis, other drugs). Stay on the line and follow their instructions.

### 2. Stay with them

Don't leave them alone, even for a few minutes. Their condition can get worse quickly.

### 3. Put them in the recovery position

If they're unconscious but breathing, roll them onto their side so that if they vomit, it drains out of their mouth instead of into their lungs:

- Kneel next to them and lay them on their back.
- Put the arm nearest you out at a right angle to their body.
- Bring their far arm across their chest and place the back of that hand against the cheek nearest you.
- Bend their far knee up, then pull on that knee to roll them toward you onto their side.
- Tilt their head back slightly and their chin forward to keep the airway open.

If they're sitting up and conscious, keep them sitting up, not lying flat on their back.

### 4. Keep them warm

Cover them with a blanket or jacket. Alcohol makes the body lose heat even when the person feels hot.

### 5. If they vomit, help keep their airway clear

Keep them on their side. Don't put your fingers in their mouth.

### 6. Give the paramedics information

Tell them what was consumed, roughly when, and anything else you know (medicines, other drugs, medical conditions). If you have the bottles or the pills, bring them.

### What *not* to do

- **Don't let them "sleep it off."** Blood alcohol can keep rising after someone passes out, and the most dangerous point may come after they've gone quiet.
- **Don't give coffee.** Caffeine doesn't lower blood alcohol, and it can make dehydration worse.
- **Don't put them in a cold shower.** It can drop their body temperature further and raises the risk of a fall or of choking.
- **Don't make them walk it off.** Movement doesn't speed up how fast the liver clears alcohol, and they may fall and hit their head.
- **Don't give them food or more water to "dilute" it** if they're very drowsy. They may choke.
- **Don't try to make them throw up.** Their gag reflex may not work properly, and they could inhale the vomit.
- **Don't give them more alcohol** ("hair of the dog") or any medicine to help them sleep.

## Why Blood Alcohol Keeps Rising After the Last Drink

This is the single most important thing most people don't know. When you drink, alcohol travels from your stomach and small intestine into your bloodstream over time. That means the drinks someone had in the last 30 to 90 minutes are still being absorbed after they stop.

So a person who seemed "drunk but okay" when they passed out can become dangerously intoxicated an hour later, while everyone assumes they're just sleeping. This is especially true after fast drinking: shots, chugging, drinking games, or a few strong cocktails in a short window.

The liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults, though it varies. Nothing speeds that up much. Not coffee, not water, not food after the fact, not sleep, not a shower. Time is the only thing that brings blood alcohol down, which is why the person needs to be watched while that time passes.

## Who's at Higher Risk?

Anyone can get alcohol poisoning, but these things raise the odds:

- **Drinking fast.** NIAAA defines binge drinking as a pattern that brings blood alcohol to 0.08% or higher, which for a typical adult is about 4 drinks for women or 5 for men in around 2 hours. Alcohol poisoning usually involves well beyond that, often in a much shorter time.
- **Shots, high-proof liquor, and drinking games.** These pack a lot of alcohol into minutes, before the body has a chance to show how drunk the person really is.
- **Drinking on an empty stomach.** Food slows how fast alcohol is absorbed. Without it, blood alcohol spikes faster (more on that in [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach)).
- **Smaller body size and lower tolerance.** Someone who rarely drinks, or who is lighter, will reach a higher blood alcohol level from the same number of drinks.
- **Mixing alcohol with other depressants.** Opioid painkillers, benzodiazepines (such as Xanax or Valium), sleep aids, some antihistamines, and other sedating drugs all slow breathing too. Together with alcohol, the effect can be much stronger than either alone. This combination is a common factor in deaths.
- **Mixing alcohol with energy drinks.** Caffeine can make people feel less drunk than they are, which can lead them to keep drinking.
- **Not knowing what's in your cup.** Punch bowls, jungle juice, and heavy-handed pours make it very hard to count drinks.

## "Should I Call? I Don't Want Them to Get in Trouble"

This is the most common reason people wait, and waiting is the dangerous part. A few points worth knowing:

- **Paramedics are there to treat the person, not to judge the party.** Their focus is getting the person breathing safely.
- **Many US states have medical amnesty or Good Samaritan laws** that offer some legal protection to people who call for help in an alcohol or drug emergency, and to the person who needs help. The details vary by state, and many colleges have their own amnesty policies too. Even where no such law exists, the risk of getting in trouble is far smaller than the risk of someone dying.
- **If you're not sure, call anyway.** Dispatchers and Poison Control would much rather hear from you about someone who turned out to be fine.

If the person is awake, talking, and clearly not in danger, but you're unsure how worried to be, Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) is free, confidential, and available around the clock. If any of the serious signs are present, skip that step and call 911.

## What Happens at the Hospital

Knowing what to expect can make calling feel less scary. Hospital treatment for alcohol poisoning is mostly about supporting the body until the alcohol clears. It usually involves:

- **Close monitoring** of breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, and temperature.
- **Protecting the airway.** If breathing is too slow or the person can't protect their airway, they may need oxygen or, in serious cases, a breathing tube until they recover.
- **IV fluids** to treat dehydration.
- **Checking and correcting blood sugar** and other blood chemistry.
- **Vitamins,** such as thiamine, which is often given to people who drink heavily.
- **Treating seizures** if they happen.

Contrary to what movies suggest, "pumping the stomach" is not a routine part of treatment for alcohol poisoning, because by the time someone reaches the hospital most of the alcohol has usually already been absorbed. Most people who get timely care recover, though some need to stay several hours or overnight.

## Alcohol Poisoning Myths

**Myth: If they're asleep, they're fine.** Passing out is a warning sign, not a recovery. Blood alcohol can keep rising while they sleep.

**Myth: Coffee sobers you up.** Caffeine might make someone feel more alert, but it does nothing to lower blood alcohol or reverse its effect on breathing.

**Myth: A cold shower will snap them out of it.** It can cause dangerous cooling and falls.

**Myth: Throwing up gets the alcohol out.** Vomiting mainly clears what's still in the stomach, not what's already in the bloodstream. And forcing someone to vomit when they're very drunk can cause choking.

**Myth: Experienced drinkers can't get alcohol poisoning.** A high tolerance can make someone look less drunk than they are, but it doesn't protect the brainstem in the same way. People with high tolerance can still reach dangerous levels, and they often drink larger amounts.

**Myth: You can only get it from hard liquor.** Any alcohol can do it. Liquor just makes it easier to drink a lot quickly.

**Myth: Eating bread or drinking water after the fact helps.** Food and water before and during drinking slow absorption. Once someone is severely intoxicated, they're mostly a choking risk.

## How to Lower the Risk on a Night Out

You don't need a complicated plan. The basics make most of the difference:

- **Eat a real meal before you start**, ideally with some protein and fat.
- **Pace yourself.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour, and alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink.
- **Skip drinking games and rounds of shots**, or at least sit some out.
- **Know what's in your glass.** Be cautious with mixed punches and generous pours.
- **Don't mix alcohol with sleep aids, painkillers, anxiety medications, or other drugs.** If you take a prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether it's safe with alcohol.
- **Have a buddy system.** Agree ahead of time that you'll check on each other, and that whoever's worried makes the call.
- **Make sure a drunk friend never goes to bed alone and unchecked.** If someone is very drunk, have a sober person stay with them and check their breathing.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers pacing and next-day recovery in more detail.

### Where DHM fits (and where it doesn't)

Dihydromyricetin (DHM) is a plant compound that some people take before or after drinking. There's interesting early research on how it might affect alcohol metabolism and the brain, much of it in animals, and some people find it helps with how they feel the next day. But it's important to be clear: **there is no good evidence that DHM, or any supplement, lowers blood alcohol fast enough to matter in an emergency, protects against alcohol poisoning, or makes it safe to drink more.** If someone shows the signs above, a supplement is not a substitute for calling 911.

If you're interested in DHM for ordinary next-day comfort after moderate drinking, two widely used options are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Treat it as one small part of a plan that starts with eating, pacing, and drinking less.

## The Bottom Line

Alcohol poisoning is an emergency where the brain's automatic systems, mainly breathing, start to fail. The signs are confusion, being unable to wake up, vomiting while barely conscious, seizures, slow or irregular breathing, and cold, pale, or bluish skin. If you see them, call 911, stay with the person, roll them onto their side, and keep them warm. Don't rely on coffee, cold showers, or sleep. A hangover is the next-day aftermath and is usually not dangerous, but confusion, nonstop vomiting, chest pain, or seizures the next day still need medical care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What are the first signs of alcohol poisoning?**

Early warning signs include severe confusion, slurred speech that's getting worse, vomiting, and drifting in and out of consciousness. More serious signs are being unable to wake up, slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute), pauses of 10 seconds or more between breaths, seizures, and cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin. If you see any of the serious signs, call 911.

**How do I know if it's a hangover or alcohol poisoning?**

Timing and consciousness are the clearest clues. Alcohol poisoning happens while blood alcohol is high, during or within hours of drinking, and the person is confused, unresponsive, or can't be woken. A hangover happens the next day after alcohol has mostly cleared. You feel awful, but you're awake and able to talk and think. If you're unsure, treat it as poisoning and get help.

**How long does alcohol poisoning last?**

It lasts as long as blood alcohol stays dangerously high, which can be many hours, because the liver clears alcohol at a roughly fixed rate of about one standard drink per hour for many adults. With hospital care, most people recover within a day, though they may feel very unwell afterward. Without care, the danger can peak after the person has already passed out.

**Can you sleep off alcohol poisoning?**

No. Blood alcohol can keep rising after someone falls asleep as the last drinks are absorbed, and the main dangers (slowed breathing and choking on vomit) happen while they're unconscious. Never leave a very drunk person alone to sleep it off. Stay with them, keep them on their side, and call 911 if they show the warning signs.

**How many drinks does it take to get alcohol poisoning?**

There's no single number. It depends on how fast you drink, your body size, whether you've eaten, your tolerance, and whether you've taken other drugs or medicines. Fast drinking (shots, chugging, drinking games) is the biggest risk because it raises blood alcohol faster than the body can show how drunk you are. Mixing alcohol with sedatives or opioids makes poisoning possible at lower amounts.

**What should you do if someone has alcohol poisoning?**

Call 911, stay with them, and if they're unconscious but breathing, roll them onto their side in the recovery position so they won't choke if they vomit. Keep them warm and tell paramedics what they drank and anything else they took. Don't give coffee, food, or a cold shower, and don't try to make them vomit.

**Will I get in trouble for calling 911 for a drunk friend?**

Many US states have medical amnesty or Good Samaritan laws that offer some protection to people who call for help in an alcohol emergency, and many colleges have similar policies. Rules vary by state. Either way, paramedics are focused on keeping the person alive, and the risk of not calling is far greater than any trouble from calling.

**Does DHM prevent alcohol poisoning?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM or any supplement prevents alcohol poisoning, lowers blood alcohol quickly, or makes heavy drinking safe. Only time lowers blood alcohol. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, call 911 regardless of anything they've taken.
